note.headline: Microsoft slips 1.25% to 489.93 on reported outage; support holds, hold stays
note.happening: Microsoft fell 1.25% to 489.93. That puts it back inside the 485.58–490.27 zone where it has been trading and just above the 475.34–485.06 support zone. The Verge reported that Microsoft declared a 'Code Red' after a large Outlook outage. The next earnings report is on 2027-01-27, and analysts' earnings estimates have risen 2.19% over the last 30 days.
note.business: The core business is still improving. Sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier in the latest quarter, faster than the 18.3% two quarters ago. Trailing revenue is 346.4B, up from 293.8B. The operating margin, the share of each sales dollar left after running costs, rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. The weak spot is cash. Trailing free cash flow, the cash left after spending on the business, fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and the free-cash-flow margin is only 17.31%. The filings note that each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, compared with 51¢ three years ago. In plain words, heavy spending is not paying back yet. That spending is what puts the cash and the valuation at risk. The reported Outlook outage mainly hurts sentiment and reputation. It would only become a business problem if customers left over it, and nothing in the data shows that (general knowledge). Things not at risk today: the balance sheet holds 29.0B in net cash with 64.5B of liquidity, and share count fell 0.27% over the year, so owners are not being diluted.
note.worth: There are two ways to value Microsoft here, and they disagree sharply. The cash-flow method (a discounted cash flow, or DCF: future cash brought back to today's money at a 9.9% discount rate) starts from today's 60.0B of free cash flow. It gives 183.71 in the bear case, 222.45 in the base case and 295.41 in the bull case. Working backwards, today's price only makes sense if free cash flow starts growing at about 39.3% a year. Even 30% starting growth gives a value of just 350.1. The other method compares the stock with its own past price-to-sales ratios (share price compared with sales per share). That gives 474.82 at the low end, 534.4 in the middle and 591.77 at the high end. The price of 489.93 sits near the bottom of that range. Against similar companies the stock looks expensive: it trades at 10.5 times sales, while the peer median is 3.6. By earnings, the stock trades at 25.6 times trailing earnings and 20.2 times next year's estimate. The gap between the two methods comes down to one assumption: whether today's lower cash flow is temporary. Two of the three measures lean expensive. I use the own-history range because it treats today's depressed cash flow as temporary, but that is a choice, not a fact.
